approachQuestion.prompt:
Energy permits

You have energy E, score 0, and permits already sorted by nondecreasing cost with positive costs. Each permit may be used at most once in either direction: spend its cost in energy to gain one score, or, if score is at least one, spend one score to gain its cost in energy. Return the greatest score obtainable at any point; unused permits are allowed.

Example 1: costs=[100,200,300,400], E=200 → 2: buy 100, sell 400, buy 200, buy 300.
Example 2: costs=[5], E=4 → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ costs[i] ≤ 10^9; 0 ≤ E ≤ 10^12. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Use two indices into the supplied sorted costs. If energy can buy the cheapest remaining permit, buy it and update the best score. Otherwise, if score>0 and at least two permits remain, sell the most expensive remaining permit; otherwise stop. Return the best score.
options.feedback: Buying a cheaper permit gains the same score while retaining more energy. When no buy is possible, selling the most expensive permit gains the most energy for the same score loss; selling the final permit cannot improve the best score. These exchanges preserve an optimal continuation.

options.text: Buy affordable permits in increasing cost order, but never sell a permit.
options.feedback: A sale can fund multiple buys. In the first example this stops at score 1, although trading a costly permit enables score 2.

options.text: Sell a permit before any purchase to maximize initial energy.
options.feedback: A sale requires positive score. For costs=[5] and E=0, selling immediately is illegal.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Each buy or sale consumes one sorted endpoint using scalar state.

The scans do not restart for each item.

details: Each buy or sale consumes one permit by moving one end inward. Across all iterations there are at most n such moves, so worst-case time is O(n). Only two indices, energy, score and best score are kept: O(1) auxiliary space. The already-sorted input is not copied and there is no recursion.
Already sorted input, iterative two-ended scan, no copying, hashing or recursion.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
